name: us-state-tax
description: Dependency-free US state AND LOCAL individual income tax engine for tax years 2025 and 2026, covering 26 states and 140 local income taxes: New York City, Yonkers, all 24 Maryland jurisdictions, all 92 Indiana counties and all 24 Michigan cities. Models what rate tables leave out: Michigan, where Detroit charges residents 2.4% on a base the MI-1040 does not contain - 60% of what the state itself charges at 100k - where the Uniform City Income Tax Ordinance excludes pensions, IRA distributions, Social Security, unemployment and military pay entirely so a city taxes a retiree at zero while the state is still working out the tier, where the personal exemption has been the $600 the Legislature set in 1964 and is worth $14.40 of tax against an indexed $5,800 state exemption, where the nonresident rate is one half of the resident rate by statute and is derived rather than stored, and where a resident working in another taxing city gets a credit capped at their OWN city's nonresident rate - so a Lansing resident commuting to Detroit pays 70% more city tax than one working at home while a Detroit resident commuting to Grand Rapids pays exactly the same; Indiana, where the average county rate is 1.914% against a state rate of 3.00% so two fifths of the bill is levied by a county, where Randolph County is at the 3.00% statutory maximum and from 2026 charges more than the state does while Porter County charges one sixth of that, and where six counties raised their rate for 2026 in the same year the state cut its own; Maryland, where every resident owes a county income tax of 2.25%-3.30% on the same taxable income - a third to two fifths of the whole bill, reported by no table of state rates - where Frederick County's bracket selects one rate that applies to the WHOLE income so one dollar at $150,000 costs $360.03 while the same dollar in Anne Arundel costs three cents, where the local earned income credit is not stored but is ten times each county rate, where the new 2% capital gains surtax is a test rather than a floor so one dollar of AGI at $350,000 can cost $6,933.08, and where the itemized deduction limit is section 68 revived by a state; Massachusetts, which every rate table reports as a flat 5% and which taxes short-term capital gains at 8.5% and long-term gains on collectibles at 12% on half the gain; New Jersey, which has no federal starting line at all and whose retirement exclusion ends in a wall that costs a joint retiree $1,381 on one dollar of income; CalEITC, which is not a percentage of the federal credit but a triangle with no plateau; California's Young Child Tax Credit; New York City's 3.078%-3.876% resident tax and its 30%-to-10% sliding earned income credit; the Yonkers surcharge of 16.75% of the state tax; New York's supplemental tax, which claws back the benefit of the lower brackets; which federal figure each state starts from; which federal deductions it adds back; the state earned income credits and the four that are not what they look like; and the credit phase-outs that make Utah's and Pennsylvania's flat taxes anything but flat. Every figure cited to the statute or state release it came from, and every carried-forward figure flagged as provisional.
